turns.content: so I got this today 🤔 default notice from my landlord for withholding the $3800 in maintenance charges from July. like, the hvac was broken for almost three weeks in a heatwave and i lost probably a third of my normal revenue. i told them i wasn't paying until it was fixed. now they're calling it a default and giving me 10 days to cure or else. am i crazy or is this straight-up retaliation for me pushing back

The sequence you described does not establish retaliation. It shows nonpayment of $3,800, then a default notice with a 10-day cure. That is the ordinary contractual response to unpaid charges under most leases. Motive is not proven by the notice itself.

You are not “crazy” for treating three weeks of failed HVAC in a heatwave as a serious problem. Withholding the charges as self-help is a separate legal act. In typical commercial leases (maintenance charges plus lost revenue point that way), the tenant’s duty to pay often continues even when the landlord’s repair duty is disputed; the usual path is pay, document, and claim damages or offset later—not stop paying. Residential rules can differ by state, but many still require a specific notice-and-repair process before any deduction. Either way, unpaid sums are commonly an event of default on their own.

What is not known, and would change the analysis: jurisdiction; whether this is commercial or residential; the exact lease clauses on HVAC, maintenance, rent/charge withholding, default, and cure; what written notice you gave about the HVAC and when; and the full text of today’s notice. Those documents—not the timing after you “pushed back”—decide whether you had a right to withhold and whether a retaliation claim is even available.

Risk if you do not cure within the stated 10 days: the landlord can typically accelerate remedies in the lease (termination, possession, damages, sometimes lockout), independent of the HVAC dispute. Ignoring the clock to argue fairness is a common way tenants lose the procedural fight.

Next step: calendar the 10-day deadline from the notice, read the notice and the lease side by side, and take both to a landlord-tenant lawyer in your jurisdiction before the period runs. Do not treat the HVAC complaint as a substitute for curing or for a court-ordered offset unless counsel confirms you have that right.

so i looked at the lease binder they attached to the notice. there's a municipal code compliance sign-off... and an invoice from their hvac contractor showing the rooftop unit was fully replaced two weeks ago with certified temp logs. so it's fixed now apparently 🤷. still doesn't undo july though

The attached papers show the rooftop unit was replaced about two weeks ago, with a contractor invoice, certified temperature logs, and a municipal code sign-off. They do not cancel the $3,800 July maintenance charges or stop the 10-day cure clock.

Your stated condition for nonpayment was that you would not pay until the HVAC was fixed. On the documents you now have, that condition has already been met, and the charges remain unpaid. A later repair does not, by itself, credit or erase a prior invoice. A July outage, if proven, is a separate damages or offset question; it is not established by post-repair logs or a code sign-off, and it is not proven by a self-estimated one-third revenue loss.

Those attachments also do not show retaliation. They are consistent with the landlord documenting that the unit is in service and treating the remaining issue as unpaid charges.

Unknowns that still control the legal result: jurisdiction; commercial vs. residential tenancy; the lease clauses on HVAC, payment, withholding, default, and cure; what written repair notice you gave and when; and the exact default-notice language and deadline date.

Continuing to withhold after a documented replacement leaves the default path intact. Paying the $3,800 inside the stated 10 days (under written protest if counsel advises that it preserves claims) and pursuing July losses with records is the lower-risk split. Contesting the default without a statute or lease clause that actually authorizes withholding is the higher-risk split.

Calendar the cure date from the notice, keep the binder, and have a landlord-tenant lawyer in your jurisdiction read the notice against the lease before that date runs.
wait, so you're saying because it's fixed now, i have to pay? even though they took three weeks and cost me thousands 🤔. that doesn't seem right. the damage was already done in july

The July outage, if it happened as you describe, does not cancel the $3,800 invoice or stop the default clock. A later repair also does not erase a prior charge. Those are separate items.

What the papers show: the rooftop unit was replaced about two weeks ago (contractor invoice, temperature logs, municipal sign-off), and $3,800 in July maintenance charges is still unpaid. The notice treats that unpaid sum as a default with a 10-day cure. That sequence is the ordinary contract path for nonpayment. It does not prove you have a right to withhold, and it does not prove retaliation.

What is not shown: a lease clause or statute that lets you stop paying maintenance charges because HVAC failed; a court or agreed offset; or records that prove a one-third revenue loss. Your estimate of lost revenue is a claim you would still have to prove. Even if proven, typical commercial leases (and many residential statutes) still require payment first, with damages pursued separately—not self-help withholding. Jurisdiction and the actual lease language control; those are still unknown.

If you do not pay or otherwise cure inside the stated 10 days, the landlord can usually use the default remedies in the lease regardless of the July dispute. Paying the $3,800 within that period, in writing and under protest if counsel says that preserves claims, then pursuing July losses with contemporaneous records, is the lower-risk split. Continuing to withhold because “the damage was already done” is the higher-risk split.

Calendar the cure date from the notice and have a landlord-tenant lawyer in your jurisdiction read the notice against the lease before that date runs.

so you're saying i basically have to eat the july losses and still pay them the full $3800? that's what it sounds like 🤔. what about the retaliation angle though, the notice came right after i complained

The notice after you refused to pay does not establish retaliation. You withheld $3,800; a default notice with a 10-day cure is the ordinary response to that unpaid sum. Timing after a complaint does not prove motive when nonpayment is already on the table.

I am not saying you must absorb July losses as a legal conclusion. I am saying two different items: (1) the $3,800 is still unpaid, the cure clock is still running, and a later HVAC replacement does not credit that invoice; (2) a July outage and lost revenue, if you can prove them, are a separate damages or offset claim. Typical leases and many statutes still require you to pay first and pursue that claim with records—not to withhold. Your “probably a third of normal revenue” figure is an estimate, not proof.

If you do not cure inside the stated 10 days, the landlord can usually use the lease default remedies even if a July claim later has some merit. Paying the $3,800 within that period (under written protest if a lawyer in your jurisdiction says that preserves claims), then pursuing July losses with contemporaneous records, is the lower-risk split. Continuing to withhold on fairness or retaliation grounds is the higher-risk split.

Calendar the cure date from the notice and have a landlord-tenant lawyer read the notice against the lease before that date runs. Jurisdiction and the actual clauses still control; those are not in the materials you described.

Three weeks of failed HVAC in July, if you can document it, is still a separate damages or offset question. It does not credit the invoice, cancel the 10-day cure, or authorize continued withholding. The papers you described show the unit was replaced about two weeks ago; that meets the condition you said you were waiting on. Your estimate of lost revenue is still an unproven claim, not a setoff.

Paying the $3,800 within that period, in writing and under protest if a landlord-tenant lawyer in your jurisdiction says that preserves claims, then pursuing July losses with contemporaneous records, remains the lower-risk split.
